title: Assessing the Readability, Credibility, and Accuracy of Online Vaccine Information for Pregnant and Lactating Individuals: A Cross-Platform Analysis
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of vaccine information across platforms; the abstract reports an explicit misinformation prevalence for social media content (38%), i.e. a share of items judged inaccurate against authoritative health evidence. Denominator sizes are not reported in the abstract, so the row is low confidence.

estimates.measure_type: % of vaccine-related social media content classified as misinformation
estimates.denominator: Vaccine-related social media content (Twitter and Facebook) published 2018-2022; number of items not reported in the abstract
estimates.definition: Claim judged inaccurate when compared against scientific evidence from authoritative health organizations
estimates.misinfo_def: No explicit definition given; "Accuracy was determined by comparing claims against scientific evidence from authoritative health organizations."
estimates.source_quote: However, social media also exhibited the highest misinformation prevalence (38%), whereas official sources maintained near-perfect accuracy (98% compliance with scientific evidence).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors compared claims against scientific evidence from authoritative health organizations (WHO, CDC given as examples of official sources). No coder count, coding protocol or inter-coder reliability reported in the abstract.
estimates.moderator_quote: A cross-sectional content analysis was conducted on vaccine-related content published between 2018 and 2022. Data were collected from official health websites (e.g., WHO, CDC), social media (Twitter, Facebook), blogs, and parenting forums. ... Accuracy was determined by comparing claims against scientific evidence from authoritative health organizations.
estimates.notes: Abstract-only source. No denominator size, no country, no sampling procedure and no reliability statistics are reported, so every moderator except topic and platform is inferred from a single methods sentence. sampling_frame coded purposive because the abstract describes selecting source types rather than a keyword harvest; keyword_topical is a defensible alternative. year set to 2022 (end of the stated 2018-2022 content window).

estimates.measure_type: DISCERN credibility score of vaccine content on blogs and parenting forums (0-80 scale), reported as a range
estimates.denominator: Vaccine-related content on blogs and parenting forums published 2018-2022; number of items not reported
estimates.definition: Credibility rated with the DISCERN instrument (and HONcode certification), not a truth/falsity judgement
estimates.misinfo_def: No explicit definition given; credibility assessed with DISCERN and HONcode
estimates.source_quote: Blogs and forums demonstrated moderate readability (FK grade level: 9.5 ± 1.4 and 8.7 ± 1.1, respectively) but varied in credibility (DISCERN scores: 40-50/80).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: DISCERN instrument plus HONcode certification, applied by the authors; no coder count or reliability reported
estimates.moderator_quote: credibility was evaluated using the DISCERN tool and HONcode certification
estimates.notes: QUALITY row per the instruction that DISCERN/GQS/JAMA-type scores are recorded as QUALITY and excluded from prevalence. It is a scale-score range, not a share, so value_pct is empty and value_kind is range_not_point. Included only because the instruction says quality-score rows are kept; an adjudicator may prefer to drop it as uninformative.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) "official sources maintained near-perfect accuracy (98% compliance with scientific evidence)" implies a ~2% misinformation rate for official health websites, but that would be a complement I computed, which R8 forbids, so no row was created. This is the main judgement call in this paper. (2) "fear-based narratives (52% of misinformation cases) and scientific distortions (29%)" are thematic shares computed inside the misinformation-only subset - they describe what the misinformation was about, not how much content was false, so they are not prevalence estimates and were not entered (they are not the falsity-within-misinfo case that R3 covers). (3) Flesch-Kincaid grade levels (11.8, 7.8, 9.5, 8.7) are readability, not veracity. (4) "only 10% of sources providing multilingual content" is an accessibility measure, out of scope. (5) The abstract reports no sample sizes anywhere, so no row has a numeric denominator; if the review requires a stated n, both rows are droppable.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of vaccine-related online content published 2018-2022, drawn from official health websites (e.g. WHO, CDC), social media (Twitter, Facebook), blogs and parenting forums. Readability by Flesch-Kincaid and SMOG; credibility by DISCERN and HONcode; accuracy by comparison of claims against scientific evidence from authoritative health organizations. One-way ANOVA and chi-square tests used. Abstract reports no sample sizes, no country, no sampling/search procedure, no coder count and no inter-coder reliability.
rob.item6_quote: Accuracy was determined by comparing claims against scientific evidence from authoritative health organizations.
rob.item10_quote: However, social media also exhibited the highest misinformation prevalence (38%), whereas official sources maintained near-perfect accuracy (98% compliance with scientific evidence).
